For forty-one years, every street in Hollins Ford was named by the same hand. Elias Marrow painted the signs in his workshop on Tanner Street, black letters on cream boards, and it was his custom to pencil his initials and the date on the back of each. This spring white reflective letters on green metal went up in their place.

For as long as anyone at the ambulance station can remember, each new driver spent a first night walking the town with an old hand, learning Marrow's boards corner by corner, and a driver who mistook a turning was walked round again until the mix-ups stopped. Residents knew the walkers by sight and would stop to point out the next corner. Those night walks ended in March, and the boards they were built around are gone.

The change began with the post office, which asked to swap the boards for signs with larger letters that its carriers could read from a van. The county's rule on reflective letters came into force a month after the order went in, and the new signs carry the county's standard letters. When the crews lifted the boards in March, most had rotted through at the edges and split as they came off. It struck me only later that the two Gates, which shared a post at the foot of the hill, carried the latest dates of all, pencilled the spring before he died and hidden on their backs for decades.

At a town meeting in April, residents voted to hang whatever could be saved in the town hall. The few boards that held together sat in storage in the depot shed through the summer, and in August they crumbled as the crew lifted them onto a truck.

I have walked the old route once since, from Tanner Street down to the Gates. On some evenings I still look up at a corner for the cream board and the black letters, the way you look for a face at the window of a house where someone used to live.

passage:
The summer I turned twelve, Mrs. Pellow next door offered to teach me to keep bees. Her two hives sat on the roof of her shed, a spot she had chosen years before to lift the bees above the fence along Tamsin Lane, and she had built both of them herself long ago. By that spring her knees stopped her at the third rung of the ladder. When my mother heard about the lessons, she asked her whether I would be in the way.

So it was I who climbed onto the shed roof each morning with the smoker, while she called instructions up from the yard. In July a swarm poured out of the far hive and settled in the pear tree by her kitchen, where I found it hanging from a low branch. We shook it into a box under the lilac by the back gate, with my mother watching from the clothesline by our back steps, while a few last bees circled under the eaves of the shed.

On still evenings the sound of those two hives carried down into the yard, and I used to lie in the grass beside the shed and listen until the light went. It was the first thing I listened for each morning and the last each night. I would give a great deal to hear the pitch of that hum again, low and steady, climbing a little on the hottest afternoons.

In August we took away the full frames and spun out the honey in her kitchen. She sold it on Saturdays at the Brackwell market and kept the table herself. In September, with the ladder beyond her, she gave both hives into the care of a keeper in Dunmore, and his truck took them away one grey morning before school.

The roof of the shed has been bare ever since, and the box we hived the swarm in went with the others. When I walk down Tamsin Lane in summer, I still stop at her gate for a moment, listening for a sound that went away to Dunmore long ago.

passage:
Mara Quill had owned Rook since April, when a gray shepherd mix at the Halvering County shelter sat down on her sneaker as if he had been expecting her. He kept that habit, sitting on people's feet whenever he could. In August she entered him in the Novice class of the county obedience trial, held on the fair's last morning, hours before the closing fireworks. The hard part was the recall. Rook had to stay where she left him across the ring until she called, and in practice he kept getting up early and trotting over before she said a word.

Mara practised at Linden Park, beside the field where her brother Theo's soccer team met and across the road from the fairgrounds, where workers tested the loudspeaker every afternoon. When Rook kept breaking, she began giving the command softly, almost under her breath. Rook broke just as often. At the shelter's Tuesday class, Mrs. Ostrander, the trainer, saw him jump at a slammed door and told Mara to practise during the loudspeaker tests. So each afternoon they crossed the road and worked beside the fairground barns, and within two weeks the squeals barely turned his head.

Through all of it, Rook kept his old habit. After every recall he swung around and sat on both of Mara's sneakers, heavy and settled, while she fished a liver treat from her pocket. On hot days they rested in the strip of shade under the cattle barn, whose tin roof came down at a steep pitch almost to the ground, and he sat on her feet there too.

At the trial, the loudspeaker blared twice during the recall, and Rook sat through both blasts until Mara lifted her hand and called him. The judge awarded him a green ribbon, and at the ring gate he sat squarely on Mara's feet again. Theo asked whether they should stop at the shelter on the way home to show everyone. Mara looked down at Rook. "The old kennel row where he first sat on my sneaker was torn down in June, and I keep picturing him in that last run by the window."

passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. As the sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank of tall windows along the school's west wall goes dark, and the first swifts drop into the chimney. By the time the church clock strikes seven, every bird is inside, well before the last children leave the schoolyard, the last bus passes the school gates and the streetlights on the hill come on.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his first notebooks record a roost of nine and ten thousand birds. This year's best was 640. He keeps the old notebooks in a drawer now, and says the one in his pocket will last him the rest of his life.

In the storm two winters ago, a crack opened near the top of the chimney, and before morning the whole top third had fallen into the schoolyard. Reyburn knew the council would vote to cap the stump rather than have it pulled down, since capping cost less, and it did. The masons relaid the top courses in lime mortar rather than cheap cement and set a smooth stone cap over them, leaving the flue open. The stump is sound.

The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good. The shortened flue holds a few hundred birds at most.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and in May they will return to the same stump. Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.
